Jidlaph
JID-laf
n. (the seventh son of Nahor by Milcah, named once)
Hebrew Yidlaph, he weepeth, or he droppeth, from dalaph, to drop, to drip, or to melt away in tears; named once, Genesis 22:22.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jidlaph is the seventh of the eight sons borne to Nahor by Milcah, and he is named in a single line of a single verse: “And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel” (Genesis 22:22). Nothing else is recorded of him — no deed, no dwelling, no descendant. He is a name in a list, and the list is the point. The notice comes immediately after the binding of Isaac, and it comes as news carried to Abraham: “And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor” (Genesis 22:20). Abraham had just been given his son back from the altar; now he is told that his brother's house in Mesopotamia is multiplying. The register exists to reach the last name in it: “And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother” (Genesis 22:23). Jidlaph is one of the seven brothers God passed over on the way to the bride of Isaac. The LORD was arranging a marriage two chapters before the servant was sent, and He did it by giving a man eight sons in a far country. Jidlaph never knew he was in the story.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Jidlaph, the seventh son of Nahor by Milcah, named once, Genesis 22:22; the name signifies weeping or dropping.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yidlaph, he weepeth, or he droppeth.

From dalaph, to drop, to drip, or to melt in tears.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, Genesis 22:22.

He is the seventh of the eight sons of Nahor by Milcah.

The list exists to name Bethuel, and through Bethuel, Rebekah.

Key Scripture

Gen 22:22 — "And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel."

Gen 22:20 — "And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor;"

Gen 22:23 — "And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother."

Gen 24:15 — "And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder."

Modern Corruption

Genealogies are dismissed as filler; Genesis 22 shows a list of forgotten names doing the quiet work of providence toward a marriage God had already appointed.

expand to see more

The modern reader skips the lists, and the historical-critical handling of them goes further: it treats such registers as late tribal etiology rather than record. Scripture treats them as record, and as record with a purpose. The eight names of Genesis 22:22-23 are not decoration around Rebekah; they are the evidence that God had been building a household in Haran all the while Abraham was walking to Moriah. The chapter that shows the father of the faithful raising the knife ends by showing the LORD quietly stocking a well in Mesopotamia with the girl who would carry the promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence works through the unrecorded. Seven of Milcah's eight sons contribute nothing to the narrative except the fact of their existence, and that fact establishes the eighth. A believer whose life leaves no line in any chronicle is not therefore outside the work; he may be the seventh name in a verse that exists to reach the eighth.
